books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

primary_sources: James K. Polk, Fourth Annual Message to Congress, December 5, 1848

stimulus.source_note: James K. Polk, Fourth Annual Message to Congress, December 5, 1848. Public domain.
stimulus.text: The accounts of the abundance of gold in that territory are of such an extraordinary character as would scarcely command belief were they not corroborated by the authentic reports of officers in the public service, who have visited the mineral district, and derived the facts which they detail from personal observation.

source: original; stimulus is a verbatim excerpt from James K. Polk, Fourth Annual Message to Congress, December 5, 1848, public domain
stem: The message suggests that the gold reports were first met with which reaction?

options.misconception: Polk says the accounts were extraordinary and hard to believe, not that people ignored them.
Nothing in the message suggests Congress was angry; Polk is reporting news, not answering a charge.

options.text: Fear that Mexico would retake California.
options.misconception: California was already American by treaty in 1848; the message raises no fear of Mexico retaking it.

options.text: Disbelief that the accounts could be true.

rationales.A: Polk says the accounts were so extraordinary they would “scarcely command belief” — doubt, not indifference.
rationales.B: The message reports welcome news to Congress; there is no sign of anger in it.
rationales.C: By December 1848 the treaty had given California to the United States; Mexico retaking it is not raised.
rationales.D: Polk says the accounts “would scarcely command belief” without corroboration — people doubted the gold stories at first.
rationales.general:
1. Find Polk's own words about the reports. He says they were “of such an extraordinary character as would scarcely command belief.”
2. Read that plainly. People heard the gold stories and did not believe them.
3. Check the rest. No indifference, no anger, and no fear of Mexico appears in the message.
Remember: “scarcely command belief” is a careful way of saying nobody believed it. Polk's whole message is the answer to that doubt.
